inline.s: In addition, you may also inquire: What is the present thought? This too is a very effective point of entry. Especially when obsessive thinking arises, inquire into this huatou and watch how thought after thought appears. If you truly fix your gaze on it, it will vanish. If it arises again later, inquire once more: What is the present thought? In this way obsessive thinking will not run wild and become a flood; you will be spared much pointless suffering, and your power in practice will grow swiftly. This is the wondrous method that turns iron into gold and transforms harm into benefit. When a deluded thought arises, this is karma coming to bind the mind; when the deluded thought ceases, this is the mind turning karma around. Deluded arising and deluded ceasing—this is the crucial point of doing the work.

[Obsessive thinking] means that a certain idea or concept appears repeatedly in the patient’s mind, accompanied by a subjective sense of being compelled and by suffering. The patient is fully able to recognize that the thought is unnecessary or absurd, and tries hard to drive such thoughts out of the mind, yet cannot freely interfere with or control them. Hence the frequent experience of “not being able to control it,” together with irritability and anxiety: there is both self-compulsion and counter-compulsion.

Psychologists divide a person’s knowledge and skills into three adjacent concentric rings: the innermost ring is the “comfort zone,” the knowledge and skills we have already mastered; the outermost ring is the “panic zone,” the knowledge and skills we cannot yet learn; and the ring between them is the “learning zone.” Only by practicing within the learning zone can a person make progress. Effective practice tasks must be carried out precisely within the trainee’s “learning zone.”

Scientists studied the training of figure skaters and found that, within the same practice time, ordinary skaters prefer to practice the moves they mastered long ago, while top skaters spend more time practicing jumps of every degree of difficulty. Ordinary enthusiasts play golf purely to enjoy the process of hitting the ball, while professional players concentrate on practicing difficult shots from every kind of extremely uncomfortable position. Genuine practice is not about completing a quota of exercise; the essence of practice is to keep doing the things you cannot yet do well.

Therefore the Chan practitioner must be highly targeted in his own practice and study. If he always cultivates within the comfort zone, he will stand still and stagnate on the path; if he grits his teeth and toils hard within the panic zone, body and mind will be depleted, and in time he will grow weary and retreat. So one should practice within one’s own learning zone, and once it is mastered, not spend further time on it but move at once to the next level of difficulty. Then the panic zone close at hand becomes the learning zone. Thus in practice and study one must know the stages, and must also know when to turn. Step by step firmly planted, straight on to the treasure ground.

Removing deluded thoughts is like quitting a drug: in the process of ten thousand thoughts returning to one and of the one returning to nothing, you will encounter the distress of withdrawal. You need only recognize that these are the symptoms of withdrawal (the removal of deluded thoughts), and persevere with unshakable determination and skillful means—victory lies just ahead.

blocks.text: Chapter Two: The One Returns to Nothing

inline.s: Surrender to the present moment, be present and observe the mind, do not think.
Why so restless—whither would you go?
The wild mind does not rest; once it rests, that is bodhi.
Observe your reactions as thoughts, emotions, and events arise.
If a deluded thought arises, return at once to the present moment, and the deluded thought ceases of itself.

[Surrender to the present moment] To accept the present moment without aversion, without resistance, without rejection—that is to say, forbearance, compliance, not grasping at marks, immovable as suchness. [Non-resistance] Non-resistance does not necessarily mean doing nothing; it means that no action arises from habitual reaction. When you are in a state of intense presence and “do nothing,” that is, for situations and for people, a powerful force of transformation and healing. [Why so restless—whither would you go?] Why is your mind unsettled—where is it you want to go? [Mind unsettled, wanting to go somewhere] Most people regard this present moment in one of three ways: as a transition toward a goal, as an obstacle, or as an enemy; and they do not know
how to abide in the present moment

. To abide in the present moment is to fully accept what the present moment is (without aversion, without resistance, without struggle) and, with focused attention, to do what you ought to do—this is cultivation. Then impatience, depression, and stress vanish along with it.

When the work of “ten thousand thoughts returning to one” is accomplished, you have the foundation to enter the stage of cultivating “the one returning to nothing.” “The one returning to nothing” is the work of no-thought—abiding enduringly in the state of “no-thought, and clearly knowing that it is no-thought.” Be ever diligent and never slack; practice it long, until movement and stillness are one and all is a single piece.
The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
“What is meant by the meaning of enlightenment is that the essence of mind is free from thought.”
This is to say:
the essence of mind being free from thought is enlightenment.
The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana
says elsewhere:
“If there are sentient beings who can observe no-thought, then they are oriented toward the Buddha’s wisdom.”
Master Hanshan, in his Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, comments:
This proves that no-thought is the shortcut to Buddhahood!

It means that not only do bodhisattvas cultivate cessation, so that they arrive at no-thought and this is named the ultimate; even ordinary sentient beings, if in the twenty-four hours of the day they can observe no-thought, then thought after thought they move toward the Buddha’s wisdom! There is no essential for attaining Buddhahood that surpasses this, and so it is specially revealed here.”
It says elsewhere:
“All defiled dharmas arise in dependence on fundamental ignorance, and fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of thought. Because
(since)

sentient beings have from the first never been free from thought, it is said that ‘all defiled dharmas are marks of non-enlightenment.’ The meaning makes plain that if one understands no-thought, then all afflictions are cut off at once; hence this concluding passage points to the first single thought as the root of the suffering of birth and death, wishing to enable practitioners to see suffering and know its cause,
and to know that freedom from thought is the essence of cultivation

[Cultivating cessation] Where wholesome dharmas have already arisen, one increases cultivation of them and causes them to grow; what was not previously attained, one can cause to be present before one. All unwholesome dharmas are naturally cut off. This is named cultivating cessation.
In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha says:
“The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without marks and without thought.”
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:
“Just as you are, right here, is it; stir a thought and you have missed it.” “Still the thoughts, forget the reckonings, and the Buddha appears of himself.”
Master Hanshan says:
“By applying effort to this one point of freedom from thought, for a long time, suddenly the flow of thoughts snaps off, mind and objects are both forgotten
(interchangeable with “perished”)
, like a lion escaped from its chains, roaming at ease.”

(Translation: Because one applies effort to the single point of freedom from thought, as time goes on, suddenly the flow of thoughts snaps off; mind and objects are both perished, like a lion escaped from its chains, roaming at ease.) (From the Dream Roaming Collection
Instruction to the Chan Practitioner Liaoxin Hai)

[Mind and objects both forgotten (interchangeable with “perished”)] Mind and objects are both perished. This is the state in which subject and object are both extinguished: the observing mind and the observed object are quenched together, which is precisely the state of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.
The method of practice at this stage is:
presence observing the mind.

Because here one observes the mind while in the state of presence, the effect is better than that of ordinary mind-observation. Moreover, the deeper the presence, the less easily deluded thoughts arise. When you have practiced it until it is second nature, one day there will suddenly come an occasion when deluded thoughts cease all at once: so long as you yourself do not deliberately stir a thought, you abide in the state of no-thought. Take one step further and accomplish this: thoughts are like tap water—turn it on and it flows, turn it off and it stops. This is
“Be master wherever you are; wherever you stand is true”
(the words of Linji).

Because the foundation of presence from the earlier stage of “ten thousand thoughts returning to one” is already there, it is now relatively easy to use presence observing the mind in order to accomplish the one returning to nothing.

The work of presence observing the mind can be done in two steps: first, observe whether the mind is scattered or dull. If the mind is scattered, then observe the scattering; if the mind is dull, then observe the dullness. If it is neither scattered nor dull, then simply watch it thus. When this first step has matured, you may enter the second step:
Do not think. If a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it; if the deluded thought ceases, be still and constantly aware.

[Do not think] Do not think about anything at all. This is what the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch means by “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil,” and “simply do not think of anything, good or evil.” The Sixth Patriarch says:
“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at this very moment, what is the original face of Upasaka Ming?”
(Translation: Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at this very moment (at the juncture when a single thought is not produced), which is your original face?) It says elsewhere:

“If you wish to know the essentials of mind, simply do not think of anything, good or evil, and you will naturally enter the pure essence of mind, serene and eternally still, with wondrous function as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
(Translation:

If you wish to know the essentials of mind, you need only refrain from thinking of anything, good or evil (free from marks amid marks), and you will naturally enter the pure essence of mind (the original nature), serene and eternally still, with inexhaustible wondrous function, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

[Know it and do not follow it] Watch this thought without judging it, and do not let it continue (do not give rise to thought upon thought). The key to “knowing it and not following it” is to work on the “knowing,” watching as a cat watches a mouse hole: the moment a thought arises, know it. Once you can “know it the moment it arises,” “not following it” becomes easy. [Still and constantly aware] No-thought, and clearly knowing that it is no-thought. “Constantly aware” means always knowing. The Treatise on the Cessation of Views says:
“The mind-nature being quiescent and extinguished is concentration; constantly understanding quiescence and extinction is wisdom.”

This is to say: when the mind-nature abides in the state of quiescence and extinction, this is called concentration; clearly and constantly knowing that the mind-nature is now in the state of quiescence and extinction is called wisdom. Therefore “still and constantly aware” is precisely the equal holding of concentration and wisdom.
Through observing one attains concentration; this is the samadhi of suchness, king of all samadhis, and so it is called supreme concentration. The Treatise on Generating the Bodhi Mind says:
“If a deluded mind arises
(when a thought arises)
, know it and do not follow it; when the delusion ceases
(when the thought ceases)
, the source of mind is empty and still, and all virtues are complete, with inexhaustible wondrous function.”

[Concentration] Within, one is not turned by thoughts; without, one is not dragged by objects. [Source of mind] The mind is the source of all dharmas, and so it is called the “source of mind.” [All virtues are complete] The ten thousand virtues are all complete. Si means “then” or “thus.” For example: with preparation, one can then be free of calamity.
On the cushion and off the cushion,

walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, eyes open or eyes closed, never set aside the work of presence observing the mind; the more you observe, the deeper it goes; the deeper it goes, the more you observe. Presence observing the mind is the sharp weapon for the earnest inquiry and the breaking through of the three barriers (the initial barrier, the heavy barrier, and the firm barrier) that follow below; this work must be made pure and refined. The more difficult the time and place for the work of presence observing the mind, the more you must do it, penetrating layer by layer, until you can handle it with ease.
How does one observe the mind? The Buddhadharma is vast, but its root is the mind; the gates of practice are countless, but the chief one is observation. The ancient virtuous ones say:
“If one does not observe the mind, the Dharma has no place to come from.”

By turning the light inward and illumining within, one can begin to draw forth the Buddha-nature; then all gates of samadhi, all gates of dharani, all gates of liberation, and all gates of spiritual power appear at once. Therefore observing the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddhadharma, and no other practice can match it. To observe and illumine constantly is prajna permeating ignorance. Once ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya appears at once (clarifying the mind and seeing the nature). One leaps straight into the Tathagata’s ground, and attains the dharmakaya without passing through kalpas of cultivation.
Therefore Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Treatise on Breaking the Marks says:
“The single dharma of observing the mind alone encompasses all dharmas and is the most essential and concise.”

[Dharani] Rendered into Chinese as “comprehensive retention”: “comprehensive” means to encompass all dharmas, and “retention” means to be able to hold boundless meanings. In other words, it means being able to grasp the general outline of all dharmas.
The Sutra of the Great Vehicle’s Contemplation of the Mind of the Ground says:
“Within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. Those who can observe the mind attain ultimate liberation; those who cannot remain forever in bondage.”
The Nirvana Sutra says:
“To be able to observe the mind-nature is called supreme concentration.”
The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin says:
“The hundred thousand gates of Dharma all return to the square inch
(meaning one’s own mind)

, and the numberless wondrous virtues are all in the source of mind; all gates of precepts, gates of concentration, and gates of wisdom, together with spiritual transformations, are entirely complete in yourselves and do not depart from your mind.”
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original arising, rely on perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way.”
Therefore the root of the Buddhadharma is the mind, and the root of practice is observation.

Therefore observing the mind is the most direct and sharpest method of cultivation. And presence observing the mind is even more swift and convenient. When you are present, you have already stepped out of deluded thinking. So to observe the mind while in the state of presence gives excellent results; by this means enter and maintain the state of no-thought that is still and yet illumining.

When presence observes the mind, if a deluded thought arises, it is because the observation of the mind has strayed; then, with a stark awakening, gather your attention and observe, and the deluded thought ceases at once. Remember: when a deluded thought arises, this is karma coming to bind the mind; when you are aware of it and it is gone, this is the mind turning karma around. Practice in this way, and when the work is deep, you will be able to abide for long periods in the state of “not a single thought arising, and yet seeing and hearing clearly”; even if a deluded thought occasionally arises, it will drift away and vanish. Go further and abide for long periods in the no-thought state of “not a single thought arising, and yet seeing and hearing clearly,” clearly and distinctly knowing that it is no-thought—what is called “still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still”—until movement and stillness become a single piece. The essential point of presence observing the mind is this: not let a single thought slip past, see through every single thought.

[Not let a single thought slip past] Do not let any deluded thought slide by (do not be fooled by it). [See through every single thought] Do not be shrouded by any deluded thought, do not follow its tune, do not take it as something real, and still less let it take you hostage.
Master Hanshan says:

“Therefore this one mind is vast with nothing beyond it, originally pure, perfect and luminous. If in daily use one awakens to this thought after thought, then though one dwells amid the toils of the dust, one is a person who has gone beyond the world; this is why Vimalakirti called it the non-dual Dharma gate. If the lay practitioner can embody this and practice it, then all grievances and favors, right and wrong, self and others, and the roots of affliction and feeling will, at the thought, be transformed into a treasury of light. Test every circumstance of daily use by this contemplation, and be aware of it thought after thought. If you cannot forbear patiently, and afflictions obstruct you, then the moment you see it arise, at once raise the Sixth Patriarch’s phrase ‘originally there is not a single thing’
(that is, at once raise the Sixth Patriarch’s phrase ‘originally there is not a single thing,’ and abide in the state of no-thought)

, and like the precious sword of a king of diamond, all afflictions will instantly melt like ice, and body and mind will be transformed into a cool pool. Practicing in this way, if you can be diligent without retreating, you will at once realize the great field of liberation; and why
(must you)
seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere!”
(Dream Roaming Collection · Instruction to Xu Qingzhi)
It says elsewhere:

“Now, if you wish to eliminate old karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to illumine and break through ignorance, and not allow deluded thinking to sprout and secretly grow. If, at the place where deluded thoughts arise, you can cut them off with a single thought, then the roots of karma accumulated from the past are eliminated on the spot. This is what is meant by ‘fear not the arising of a thought, fear only that awareness is late.’ If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, you will be turned by it. If in daily use, at the place where thoughts stir and move, you are aware of it thought after thought and eliminate it thought after thought, this is what is meant by ‘all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.’ Since
(because)
the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is what is meant by ‘wisdom can dispel them.’ If
(you)

day and night without letting go, you diligently observe, and do not let it pass, but simply take the place where the deluded thought arises and investigate it to the end, you will find that there is no mark of arising at all. Looking and looking, in the end it cannot be grasped. When this has gone on long and become pure and familiar, then your own mind is pure and without a thing, and the mind without a thing is true reality. If you constantly observe this mind, then what deluded thought can find room in it, and what accumulated karma can lodge there? To apply the mind in this way is called the samadhi of contemplation and illumination.”
(Dream Roaming Collection · Instruction to Dong Zhiguang)
[All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them] The Sutra of the Method of Practicing the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s Contemplation says:

“The ocean of all karmic hindrances arises entirely from deluded thinking. If one wishes to repent, one should sit upright and contemplate true reality. All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.”

[Sit upright and contemplate true reality] The continuation of Master Hanshan’s instruction says: “The mind without a thing is true reality.” (For details, see the section “The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Offenses” in
Hanshan’s Recorded Instructions

) [If day and night without letting go, you diligently observe] Here “if” is your, your meaning. For example: “Change your corvée, restore your tax, then what do you think?” (This sentence comes from Liu Zongyuan’s “The Snake Catcher’s Tale”; translation: Change your job of catching poisonous snakes, restore your taxes—what do you think of that?)

Answer: On this point, Mr. Nan Huaijin says: “In the pure prajna method of observing the mind, one observes the rising and ceasing of one’s own mental consciousness; there is originally no question of where to start the contemplation—that is fussing like an old woman over nothing! The mind is not within, without, or in between. Yet when ordinary practitioners do this contemplation, it is very easy for them to gather their attention in the head, which brings on disorders such as high blood pressure; and so, in addition, the expedient of gently contemplating at the heart is offered to everyone; and lest you not understand where the ‘heart’ is, it is specially explained that it is here at the pit of the stomach, at the hollow where the ribs meet between the two nipples. Contemplate naturally right there.” (Beginning Cultivation in Concentration and Wisdom)
[Between the two nipples] The midpoint of the line joining the two nipples, commonly called the yellow court, the heart chakra, or the heart; it is also the location of the Shanzhong acupoint.

In order to make the work of no-thought finer and more subtle, you may use the method of purifying the mind through the breath: breathe slowly with the abdomen, and in every breath know clearly within yourself whether there is a deluded thought in this breath. If combined with qigong, it can also cure illness and prolong life; hence it is said that when the body is at peace, the Way prospers. The method is this: sitting, lying, or standing are all acceptable; place the tongue against the upper palate, breathe in and out through the nose, and when you inhale you must fill completely, when you exhale you must empty completely (if you cannot manage this at first, then slow down and work up to it gradually). On the inhale, the abdomen bulges outward and the qi is received into the dantian; then exhale, and the abdomen draws inward. The breathing should be gentle and effortless. Throughout the breathing, check whether each breath has a deluded thought in it, and gradually come to a mind free of distracting thoughts; this is the key to cultivating both nature and life.
[Dantian] Here it refers to the lower dantian, which is the Guanyuan acupoint on the Conception Vessel,
three inches (four fingers’ width) below the navel

, and is the place where essence is stored. The lower dantian is the chief site for refining, gathering, and storing true qi. A person’s primordial qi originates in the kidneys and is stored in the dantian; by way of the triple burner it circulates through the whole body to propel the functional activities of the five viscera and six bowels. The strength or weakness of the human body, and life and death themselves, depend entirely on whether the primordial qi of the dantian is abundant or depleted; therefore it is very important to preserve the primordial qi of the dantian. When the primordial qi of the dantian is full and abundant, one can mobilize the body’s potential and cause true qi to circulate through the whole body. Holding the mind on the dantian can regulate yin and yang, connect the heart and kidneys, fill and open the eight vessels with true qi, restore the innate physiological functions, and promote health and longevity.

At the initial stage, in order to grasp the method of purifying the mind through the breath more easily, you may use the opening and closing of the palm (one hand or both) as an aid: on the inhale, open the palm and let the abdomen bulge outward, attending to presence; on the exhale, close the palm and let the abdomen draw inward, attending to observing the mind. Once you are skilled, the opening and closing of the palm may be done very slightly, so slightly that others do not notice. In short, comfort, convenience, and sustainability are best.
When you can already enter the state of no-thought freely, you may cultivate this:
No-thought, and be aware of that no-thought.

This is the equal holding of concentration and wisdom, the essence of Chan practice. As days pass and the work deepens, the melon ripens and the stem falls, the water arrives and the channel forms; one utterly sheds the senses and their objects and thoroughly sees the original nature.
Chan Master Baizhang, ascending the hall, said:

“The numinous light shines alone, utterly shedding the senses and their objects. The essence is revealed, true and constant, not bound by words. The mind-nature is undefiled, perfect from the start. Simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the thus-come Buddha.”
(The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source)
[Utterly shedding the senses and their objects]
The six sense faculties and the six sense objects fall away completely

. [Deluded conditions] To engage in deluded clinging; here “conditions” is a verb. [Simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the thus-come Buddha] As long as you are free of deluded clinging, you are the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “The dharma Buddha (the dharmakaya Buddha) is free from clinging.” The Diamond Sutra says: “To be free of all marks is to be named a Buddha.” [Thus-come Buddha] The Buddha who is awakened to the principle-essence of suchness, that is, the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “What is a transformation Buddha? What is a reward-born Buddha? What is a thus-come Buddha?”

What you must be careful about is this: in doing the work of the one returning to nothing, you must never lose awareness and sink into the barren emptiness of a dead mind in a forgotten form; it must be still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still.
In doing the work of the one returning to nothing, there is another good method: when a thought arises, shout “Duo!” (
duō
, a shout of rebuke). This is an interesting method, and it can be done as a game: the policeman catches the thief. Master Hanshan says:
(When a deluded thought)

arises, shout “Duo!” and with one shout it vanishes. Never suppress it, for then it will do as it pleases, like a gourd on the water. Simply cast body, mind, and world to one side, and singly and distinctly raise this one thought. Like a sword brandished across the sky, whether it be Buddha or Mara, cut it all off at once, as one cuts through tangled silk. Press on with all your strength
zǎn
, to squeeze and press)

and go forward; this is what is called the straightforward mind and right mindfulness of suchness. Right mindfulness is no-thought. To be able to observe no-thought may be called moving toward the Buddha’s wisdom.”
(Dream Roaming Collection
Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan)

[Never suppress it, for then it will do as it pleases, like a gourd on the water] Never suppress a thought, for otherwise you will follow it around; it is like a gourd on the water—press this one down and that one floats up, endless. [Like a gourd on the water] A game children love to play: pressing gourds down in water. A water jar half a person’s height is filled with water, and three or five gourds are thrown in. Often this gourd is pressed down and that gourd floats up; carefully, all ten fingers are put to use, and the situation seems to be in my control—then one moment of inattention and the whole army is routed, hands and feet in a flurry, and yet the joy is endless. [Chi li li] Also written “chi li li,” an onomatopoeic word.

Question: In movement my work of the one returning to nothing goes fairly well (for example, while walking in meditation), but when I am still it loses its power, and afflictions even rise up in my mind for no reason. What should I do?
Answer: The essential point of the one returning to nothing is this:
no-thought, and clearly knowing that it is no-thought.

Under this principle, you may try other methods, for example: be aware of the present moment itself, and become one with the present moment. It is often like this: when one method is hard to make work, try another. When that method takes hold, return to the original method, and it will work. As it is said: dharmas have no high or low; what suits the capacity is wondrous. Medicines have no noble or cheap; what matches the illness is good.

Moreover, sometimes the situation of “one point broken through, all flowers blooming” will appear. That is to say, when you are at a bottleneck, pacing back and forth and unable to advance, try several more methods. As long as one method works, keep using it. Once the bottleneck is broken through, every method will work smoothly in your hands.

As for the question of what to do about “situations in which, when the work reaches the point where outer objects no longer enter, afflictions nonetheless rise up in the mind for no reason,” Master Hanshan instructs:

“When the work reaches the point where it has power, outer objects no longer enter, and only afflictions within the mind rise up for no reason. Sometimes desires flare up, sometimes the mind grows fretful, sometimes all kinds of obstacles arise, until the mind is weary and the strength exhausted, and there is no help
(anciently the same as “help”)
for it. These are the seeds of habit from beginningless kalpas contained in the eighth consciousness
(the alaya consciousness)

, and now, pressed hard by the work, they all come forth. Here above all you must be clear: first you must be able to see through them, to pass through them; never be shrouded by them, never follow their tune, never take them as something real. Simply rouse your spirit, exert yourself bravely, raise your original huatou, and ask it
(it)

, where does it come from? What after all is it? You must resolve to see where it comes down. Press on this way, and you will make gods and ghosts weep and flee, hiding their traces. You must drive them all out and kill them all, leaving not a thread. Exert yourself in this way, and you will naturally see good news.”
(Dream Roaming Collection · Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan)
Question: How can one accomplish “seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing”?

Answer: “Seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing” is to reflect things as a mirror does, without stirring thought. When you see and hear, turn back and observe the thinker, and see what it wants to think. In this way it will instead not stir thought, and so you accomplish “seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing.” By often turning back to observe the thinker, you not only avoid being hijacked by it, but you will also experience the beauty of stillness more and more deeply. Or you may be aware of that which observes, that which listens.
Question: I am present and observing the mind within the breath: inhale—aware of the abdomen; exhale—aware of the present thought, with the breath long, fine, and even. Is it all right to do this?
Answer: Entirely all right; this is a skillful method.
The work of no-mind (no-thought) is of various kinds. In the chapter “True Mind Stilling Delusion” in A Direct Explanation of the True Mind, ten kinds are set out (for details see
A Detailed Explanation of A Direct Explanation of the True Mind
). Among them, the first is the work of awareness. This is a very effective no-thought practice:

“The first is awareness. It means that when doing the work, one ordinarily cuts off thoughts and guards against their arising. The moment a single thought is born, one breaks through it with awareness; the deluded thought is broken by awareness, and later thoughts do not arise. When this is so, this awareness-wisdom itself need not be used either; delusion and awareness are both forgotten, and this is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: ‘Fear not the arising of a thought, fear only that awareness is late.’ He also says in verse: ‘You need not seek the true; you need only still the views.’ This is the work of stilling delusion.”

(Translation: 1. Awareness. When doing the work, one ordinarily abides in the state of no-thought (ordinarily cutting off thoughts) and guards against thoughts arising at every moment. The moment a single thought is born, one at once breaks through it with awareness; the deluded thought is broken by awareness, and later thoughts do not arise. When the work is ripe, this awareness-wisdom itself need not be used either; deluded thoughts and awareness-wisdom are both perished, and this is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: ‘Fear not the arising of a thought, fear only that awareness is late.’ He also says: ‘You need not seek the true mind; you need only still the stirring of thoughts (still the views), and the true mind will appear of itself.’ This is the work of stilling deluded thoughts.)

This work has two phases, “guarding” and “letting be.” Guarding: “ordinarily cutting off thoughts and guarding against their arising; the moment a single thought is born, one breaks through it with awareness; the deluded thought is broken by awareness, and later thoughts do not arise.” Letting be: “this awareness-wisdom itself need not be used either; delusion and awareness are both forgotten.”
Master Dayu says:
“Still and illumining, illumining and still: above all, do not use effort. To become a Buddha or a patriarch, there is no other secret.”
The line in this verse, “above all, do not use effort,” is precisely “
this awareness-wisdom itself need not be used
In doing this work of awareness, one should do everything calmly and consciously; not only should one be aware the moment a single thought is born,
but in everyday dealings as well, one should still be aware thought after thought

. At first this is awareness with effort (guarding); afterward one enters awareness without effort (letting be), and so arrives at the point where one does nothing at all and yet never departs from awareness, entering of oneself into the great place of rest.
When the work has reached this point, it is recommended that you carefully study Elder Yuanyin’s
A Brief Discussion of Clarifying the Mind and Seeing the Nature
Question: How does one purify the stream of one’s own mind?

Answer: There are quite a few specific approaches. For example, you may abide in presence with focus, continuity, and endurance. If a deluded thought arises, it means awareness has strayed; with a stark awakening, take awareness back, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. Not let a single thought slip past, see through every single thought. Practice it long, until it becomes effortless. The equal holding of concentration and wisdom introduced below is also a very effective method.

Of course, you may also play a game: follow your thoughts. But you must clearly know that you are following; then you will discover that as long as you follow while awake and clear, thoughts cannot control you, and may even fail to flow on. So observing the stream of your own mind (watching how it flows) is an interesting game and also a very effective method of practice.
Question: May I cultivate “the one returning to nothing” by gazing at light with the wisdom eye (the third eye between the two eyes)?

Answer: Yes. The light you observe is an object for settling the mind; when the mind is fixed on one point, there is nothing that cannot be done. While gazing at the light, be focused, continuous, and enduring, and do not let deluded thoughts arise.

Question: Why is it that although I clearly know that “all that has marks is false and delusive,” when I meet circumstances and conditions I am still turned by marks, and want to be free of them but cannot be?

Answer: This is because the power of wisdom and the power of concentration are not sufficient. So it is not enough to be free of marks by intellectual understanding alone. Cultivating “the one returning to nothing” is precisely to strengthen the power of concentration and the power of wisdom (wisdom born of concentration), so as to accomplish “knowing the illusory (wisdom) and at once letting go (concentration).”
Question: I can observe the mind briefly, but after a slightly longer time, as I observe, I lose track of what is happening. What should I do?

Answer: In order to get through this difficult pass, you may adopt the method of observing the mind with the breath: for the breathing, still use the abdominal breathing from the chapter “Awareness of the Breath.” With each inhale (or each exhale), observe with focused attention once. This is a pulsating mode of observation. Since you can already observe the mind briefly, observing in this way will give very good results. When you have practiced it until it is familiar, gradually make the transition to normal, sustained mind-observation. In order to shorten the transition time, besides your regular periods of practice, you should also fit in breath-and-mind observation at every opportunity in daily life. One of the secrets of practice is this: when the step is too high, never be discouraged, and still less give up; instead, adapt to the occasion and set up one or several auxiliary steps, and climb up rung by rung. I recall that a famous Russian writer once told a story from his past that is quite instructive:

When I was small, I was worst at mathematics, and so my mathematics teacher called my father to the school and told him gravely: this child cannot be taught! But my father was unwilling to give up, and through a friend’s introduction he found the most formidable mathematics teacher in the whole city to tutor me. Every day after school I went straight to his place and studied for an hour. On the first day, this teacher told me: forget everything you have learned before; we start from the beginning, and you follow me in everything. Seeing how fierce he looked, I did not dare make a sound, and indeed from then on I followed him in everything, not daring the slightest negligence. He taught me from the very beginning. Previously I felt that mathematics class was simply impossible to follow, still less to do the exercises; the time was truly hard to endure! This teacher, though frightening in appearance, explained things simply and set exercises that were not hard (this is where a clear teacher shows his brilliance: teaching according to the student’s capacity, he set up a series of auxiliary steps for this student with a poor foundation, so that he could climb rung by rung; add to that strict supervision, and there is no student who cannot be taught), and so the hour was not hard to endure. Later I gradually discovered that mathematics really does have its own logic, and is not a mess, and so I began to take an interest in it. The mathematics teacher at school gradually became kinder to me as well, and I too began to answer questions on my own initiative, and even worked out problems on the blackboard in front of the whole class. One day, the teacher who was tutoring me asked my father to come to his place, and told my father in front of me: this child need not come again. In fact, until I graduated from primary school, my mathematics was among the best in the class.

Question: My work of presence observing the mind was going along smoothly, when suddenly some events from the past rushed into my mind and would not leave; they tormented me for several days and left me exhausted. If this happens again in the future, what should I do?

Answer: These are karmic seeds in the alaya consciousness, now pressed out by the work. This is an obstacle and difficulty on the way to progress, and also your best training partner, helping you to leap over the dragon gate. If this happens again in the future, or even when “afflictions within the mind rise up for no reason, or desires flare up, or the mind grows fretful,” you still simply are present and observe the mind: without resisting, without rejecting, without thinking, watching it from the opposite shore as you would watch a fire, watching it patiently, until it collapses and falls apart.

Question: The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original arising, rely on perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way.” How does one accomplish the perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment?

Answer: The mark of pure enlightenment is the quiescent and extinguished mark of the self-nature’s intrinsic enlightenment, that is, the state in which the self-nature abides in no-thought. Thoughts of the mind are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For example, for one who recites the Buddha’s name, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is a fine thought. Subtle thoughts are the subtle rising, ceasing, and flowing of the consciousness-mind, which are the marks of the alaya consciousness. Ordinarily, when both coarse and fine thoughts have ceased, this is called no-thought; this is no-thought as commonly spoken of. Further, if the subtle thoughts also cease, this is ultimate no-thought. The way to begin the work of perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment is this:
no-thought, and turn the light back to illumine that no-thought.

No-thought is precisely the mark of pure enlightenment; to turn the light back and illumine that state of no-thought is to be aware of and illumine that mark of pure enlightenment. At first, the no-thought spoken of means the no-thought in which both coarse and fine thoughts have ceased, and there is still that which illumines and that which is illumined. As the work deepens, until subject and object are both perished and the subtle flowing is entirely quiescent, this is the perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment, the eternal cutting off of ignorance, and the accomplishment of the Buddha-way.
[The mark of pure enlightenment] The quiescent and extinguished mark of the self-nature’s intrinsic enlightenment. Master Hanshan’s Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Therefore all Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original arising for Buddhahood, have no other dharma, but all rely on the light of this perfect enlightenment of the self-nature, turning back to illumine the quiescent and pure essence-mark of enlightenment, which is the essence of the nature itself. When this illumines perfectly and penetrates without remainder, then ignorance is forever cut off and the dharmakaya is perfectly realized. There is only this one dharma, and so it is said, ‘all rely on perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way.’”

[Intrinsic enlightenment] The essence of mind of sentient beings (the self-nature) is by nature pure, free from all deluded marks, luminous and numinous, and possesses the virtue of awareness. This is the intrinsic virtue of the nature of the mind-essence, and so it is called intrinsic enlightenment. Yet this mind-essence of intrinsic enlightenment has, since beginningless time, been covered by ignorance and affliction, hidden away until today; once it relies on the work of cultivation and purification, it first manifests its virtue of nature, and this is called initial enlightenment. The Awakening of Faith says:

“The essence of mind is free from thought; being free from the marks of thought, it is equal to the realm of space and pervades everywhere. The single mark of the dharma-realm is the Tathagata’s equal dharmakaya; in reliance on this dharmakaya, it is named intrinsic enlightenment.”
On how to pass from awareness and illumination into perfect illumination, Mr. Xu Hengzhi has a passage of great penetration in his book
How to Practice the Buddhadharma

In summary, the elimination of habitual tendencies has the following course: ordinary people are afflicted by deluded thoughts all day long, taking the deluded as real, and always fall into the maze of subjectivity without knowing it. Once, through suffering, they begin to feel, and know that deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies do no small harm, they are willing to practice the Buddhadharma as an antidote. But in the early stages of practice, their state of mind is bound to be half-believing and half-doubting, now clear and now dim; they have understanding only, with no experiential proof. When they speak of precepts, they lean toward the outward marks; when they speak of concentration, they cling to dead stillness; when they speak of wisdom, they use the mouth-habits of the Chan school. When habitual tendencies come, they still have no strength to contend with them. This is precisely “
(precepts, concentration, and wisdom)
present when spoken of, absent when used.”

After devoted and single-minded practice of the Buddhadharma, and after hundreds and thousands of temperings and resistances, the state of mind gradually opens up and strength gradually becomes sufficient, and one can awaken to and see one’s own original essence.

At this point one knows that all right and wrong, favorable and adverse, beautiful and ugly, love and hate, and so on, are nothing but the deluded discriminating activity of one’s own mind; one can refrain from following their flow, and gradually eliminate one’s own habitual tendencies.

Thus habitual tendencies turn from coarse and heavy to fine and light, from long-lasting to short-lived, from thick to thin, from great matters to small matters, from forced to natural, from powerless to powerful, from deliberate to unnoticed. In short, the root of habitual tendencies has been loosened, and is no longer as solidly clung to as before. Continuing in this way to sweep away habitual tendencies with prajna, the power of concentration and wisdom grows daily stronger, with a momentum that nothing can withstand; one can perfectly illumine one’s own habitual tendencies everywhere and become enlightened at every moment, and the self-nature gradually becomes a single undifferentiated, perfectly luminous whole, utterly still with not a single thought, and yet vividly alive and inconceivable. One need not deliberately gather it in; the mind is naturally free of distraction. When a habitual tendency comes, one turn and it is utterly ungraspable, impossible to lay hold of. Delusion, of course, cannot grasp it; enlightenment cannot touch it either. Neither moving nor still, neither ordinary nor holy, beyond thought and words—this is precisely what is called “perfect enlightenment.”
In cultivating any Dharma gate, one cannot do without awareness and illumination. For when mind and object meet,
if there is no illumination, there is no turning

; if there is no turning, there is no emptiness; if there is no emptiness, there is no concentration; if there is no concentration, there is no wisdom. In the course of sweeping away habitual tendencies, the progress of the power of awareness and illumination can be divided into the following levels:
1. The mind arises first and awareness-illumination follows after, and it must be roused with all one’s strength;
2. Though awareness-illumination still comes after the arising of the mind, it can be roused without much effort;
3. At the arising of the mind one can be aware and illumine, but there is still a slight before and after;
4. When the mind arises, awareness-illumination arises at the same time;
5. Awareness-illumination comes first and the thought of the mind follows after, but sometimes one still forgets to illumine;
6. Awareness-illumination can always be in front, but one still has to attend to the awareness-illumination; (the above are stages of effort)
7. One does not know there is illumination, yet one has never departed from it; one clearly knows there are objects, yet originally there is no obstruction;
8. One enters the ground of constant stillness and constant illumination.
We can examine ourselves: which of these states have we actually reached
Master Dayu says:
Still and illumining, illumining and still;
to become a Buddha or a patriarch, there is no other secret.

In doing the work of no-thought, there are generally two paths. One is: look at where the thought arises. This path is rather steep; though its effect is more marked, it makes higher demands on one’s foundation. Those whose foundation is insufficient cannot begin, and even if they can begin, it is hard to sustain. The other path is: attend only to awareness, and pay no attention to deluded thoughts. Deluded thoughts arise because awareness is not focused and continuous enough. So when doing the work, ask only whether awareness is present, and do not bother about whether deluded thoughts are present; for as long as awareness is present, there are no deluded thoughts, and deluded thoughts arise in the gaps when awareness is absent. What is called “the work becoming one piece” is simply that there are no longer any gaps in which awareness is absent, and so one abides in a stable state of no-thought. Working single-mindedly on awareness in this way, practicing it long, when awareness becomes focused, continuous, and enduring, deluded thoughts naturally do not arise. It is like ordinarily attending only to raising the cat well, and paying no attention to the mice. When the cat is grown, the mice no longer come. This path is comparatively gentle and makes no great demands on one’s foundation.

In this book many methods of no-thought have been introduced; as it is said, “Everywhere the green willows can tether a horse; every road leads to Chang’an.” The point is that each person must find his own point of entry.
What is called inquiry is
turning back to look at your own original face
, so as to clarify the mind and see the nature (thoroughly see the original nature); this is the core of Chan inquiry.
“Turning back to look at your own original face” means gathering your spirit (focusing) and turning the light back to illumine, peering into (qù) the question: what is the original face?
To be in the state of peering inquiry while not a single thought arises is the doubt-sensation. Make the doubt-sensation become a stretch, a piece, a mass (enveloping the whole body).

Therefore the doubt-sensation is precisely non-arising and non-ceasing. The “non-arising and non-ceasing” spoken of here means: not a single thought arises, and awareness does not cease (not restless, not dull, not clinging to stillness, not falling into emptiness).
[Restlessness] The mind is agitated.
Turning back to look at your own original face is simply taking good care of this “non-arising and non-ceasing,”
not parting from it in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; not neglecting it in cold or heat, day or night.
This is what The Essentials of Mind Cultivation calls “awakening to this and guarding it.”
The Essentials of Mind Cultivation says:
“One who awakens to this
(the original mind)
and guards it sits in suchness without moving, in liberation; one who is deluded about this and turns away from it goes to the six destinies
(the six paths)
and revolves through kalpas of birth and death.”
(For details see
A Detailed Explanation of The Essentials of Mind Cultivation
[Not parting from it in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
not neglecting it in cold or heat, day or night
] Chan Master Gaofeng says:
“In the twelve hours of the day, do not let there be a gap. When you get up at the fourth watch, at once grope for the huatou
(the huatou here is what this text calls the doubt-sensation—peering inquiry without deluded thoughts)

, and set it right before you. If you feel at all sleepy, then get up and set foot on the ground, and it is still the huatou. When walking, do not part from the huatou at any step. When opening your mat and spreading your bowls, when lifting the spoon and setting down the chopsticks, and in all the affairs of following the community, never part from the huatou. Day and night, it is likewise. When it becomes a continuous piece, there is no one who does not awaken
(no one who does not clarify the mind and see the nature)

The essential point is this: gather your spirit (focus) and turn the light back to illumine, and with focus, continuity, and endurance peer into what the original face is, so as to deepen the doubt-sensation and take good care of it; as it is said, “great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening.”
In the course of Chan inquiry, awakening comes from doubt (the doubt-sensation), and doubt comes from faith. It is very important that faith be sincere and firm.
Chan Master Gaofeng says:

“You should know that doubt takes faith as its essence, and awakening takes doubt as its function. With ten parts of faith, there are ten parts of doubt; with ten parts of doubt, there are ten parts of awakening; it is like the water rising and the boat rising with it.”
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao)
Master Hanshan’s Dream Roaming Collection · Biography of Master Yungu says:
“Whenever anyone came to inquire, as soon as he saw him, the master
(Master Yungu)
would ask: ‘How goes your daily practice
(how is your practice ordinarily)
?’ Whether noble or humble, monastic or lay, once they entered his room he would throw a sitting cushion on the ground and have them sit upright,
turning back to look at their own original face

, and sometimes for a whole day and night not a word was spoken. On parting he would always enjoin: ‘Do not let a day pass in vain.’ On meeting again, he would always ask: ‘Since we parted, how has your practice of the mind gone—easy or difficult?’”
Chan Master Linji, ascending the hall, said:
“On the lump of red flesh there is a true person without rank, who constantly comes and goes through the faces of all of you; those who have not yet verified it
(those who have not yet seen the nature)
, look!”
(The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source)
When the Sixth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to Huiming, he said:
“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at this very moment
(at the juncture when a single thought is not produced)
, what is the original face of Upasaka Ming
(which is your original face)
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)
[At this very moment] Mr. Liu Zhuyuan says:
“In this public case
(“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at this very moment, what is the original face of Upasaka Ming?”)

the most important thing is the three characters ‘at this very moment’; this is the secret of the Chan school. If a person who has aroused the mind can abide in the mind thus, awakening is not far off. The patriarch says: ‘At this very moment is called the time before the Buddha was born.’ It is also called: ‘Dwelling at the summit, precious beyond compare.’ Only when one can abide in the mind thus for several hours a day does one meet the standard.
There will naturally be a causal occasion for the spark

, and one need not have anyone’s guidance. The patriarch says: ‘If only you can be at this very moment, you need not worry about not awakening thoroughly.’ This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-dharma; practice it with all your strength.”
(The Essentials of the Buddhadharma)

Turning back to look at your own original face takes not a single thought arising as its precondition, and to have not a single thought arise, one must first put down all conditions. Therefore “put down all conditions, not a single thought arises” is the precondition for inquiry. (Awareness Chan accomplishes “put down all conditions, not a single thought arises” through the two stages of “ten thousand thoughts returning to one” and “the one returning to nothing.”)
Elder Xuyun instructs:

“The two phrases ‘put down all conditions, not a single thought arises’ are truly the precondition for Chan inquiry. If these two phrases are not accomplished, then not only will Chan inquiry fail to succeed—it cannot even begin. For
(a conjunction, indicating cause)

with all conditions entangling you and thought after thought arising and ceasing, can you still speak of Chan inquiry? ‘Put down all conditions, not a single thought arises’ is the precondition for Chan inquiry; since we know this, how then can it be accomplished? For those of the highest capacity, a single thought rests forever, until the unproduced, and they at once realize bodhi, with no entanglements at all
(no fuss)
. Next, there is
the removing of matters by principle

. One understands that the self-nature is originally pure; affliction and bodhi, birth-and-death and nirvana, are all merely provisional names, and have nothing whatever to do with my self-nature. Everything and every thing is a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. This physical body of the four great elements, together with mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are within the self-nature like floating foam on the sea, rising and ceasing as they will, without obstructing the essence.
One should not give rise to liking and disliking, accepting and rejecting, as all illusory matters arise, abide, change, and cease.

Put it all down through and through, as if you were a dead man; then naturally the faculties, objects, and consciousness-mind subside, and greed, hatred, delusion, and craving are extinguished. All the aches and pleasures of this body, hunger and cold, fullness and warmth, honor and disgrace, life and death, fortune and misfortune, good and ill luck, praise and blame, gain and loss, safety and danger—put them all beyond your concern; only then does it count as putting down. One putting down, all putting down, forever putting down—this is called putting down all conditions. When all conditions are put down, deluded thoughts cease of themselves, discrimination does not arise, and clinging is left far behind; at this point not a single thought arises, and the light of the self-nature is fully revealed. When you have come to this, the conditions for Chan inquiry are complete, and only then, applying yourself to genuine inquiry, do you have a share in clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.”
(Elder Xuyun’s Expedient Instructions
The Preconditions for Chan Inquiry)
[Floating foam (ōu)] Bubbles on the surface of water. Because they easily arise and easily cease, they are often used as a metaphor for the impermanence of worldly affairs and the brevity of life.

This instruction is very penetrating, and Chan practitioners should take it as their own motto, often reciting it, measuring themselves against it, and testing themselves by it. The elder, with weighty earnestness, enjoins:
“If these two phrases
(put down all conditions, not a single thought arises)

are not accomplished, then not only will Chan inquiry fail to succeed—it cannot even begin. For with all conditions entangling you and thought after thought arising and ceasing, can you still speak of Chan inquiry

Turning back to look at your own original face is a good method of Chan inquiry. In fact, the whole process of Chan inquiry can be threaded through with “turning back to look at your own original face”; it is the simplest and most direct, just as Master Yungu taught above.
When the self-nature is deluded,

one takes the physical body (the four great elements) as oneself and thoughts (the shadowy traces of the six sense objects) as one’s own mind, and thinks that the physical body and thoughts are I—this is the mark of self (the small self). The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for other directions, deludedly taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six sense objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; the diseased one deludedly clings to them. Because of deluded clinging, he is not only confused about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also deluded about where those real flowers arise. From this delusion there is falsely the turning around in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.”

Once the mark of self is established, the marks of person, of sentient beings, and of a life span arise along with it. Therefore the key to being free of the four marks is to be free of the mark of self. (For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
In Eckhart Tolle’s
A New Earth (Awakening to Your Life’s Purpose)
, the structure, characteristics, and harm of the small self (the mark of self) are discussed in detail in modern language, and are worth consulting.
Master Guifeng says:

“All dharmas are like a dream—all the sages say so. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally quiescent, and the objects of dust are originally empty. This empty and still mind is luminously aware and not darkened. This empty and still knowing is your true nature. Let it be deluded or awakened, the mind knows itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’
(the knowing of empty stillness)

is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion, one deludedly clings to body and mind as I, and gives rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, and so on. If one meets a good friend who instructs one, one suddenly awakens to this empty and still knowing. This knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of self or the mark of person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, one is aware; being aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here. Therefore, though one cultivates all practices, one takes no-thought as the teaching. When one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought
(when one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought)

, then love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are not marks, one naturally practices the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end. When arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, functioning inexhaustibly, and this is named Buddha.”
(A General Preface to the Collected Interpretations of the Source of Chan)

[The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders] This is to say: the knowing of empty stillness is the gate of all wonders. [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, one is aware; being aware of it, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here] When you awaken to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind of itself is without thought. If a deluded thought arises, you must at once awaken to the fact that this is taking the illusory as real and being turned by illusory marks. Once you awaken to this, the deluded thought vanishes at once. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here! [Being aware of it, it is gone] There are two methods for “being aware of it, it is gone”: first, as soon as you notice a deluded thought, at once stop it with the power of concentration; second, as soon as you notice a deluded thought, at once take the deluded thought as the material for contemplation: why did this deluded thought arise? What has it to do with me? Is there any need to think it through further? When you think it through deeply and thoroughly, the deluded thought ceases of itself (this is weakening and even uprooting the karmic seeds).
Therefore the knowing of empty stillness is the state of the original mind, while seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the state of the consciousness-mind.

When the self-nature is awakened, one takes the dharmakaya as oneself and the knowing of empty stillness as one’s own mind, and uses the physical body and thoughts as tools for practicing, for liberating sentient beings, and for handling the affairs of daily life.

[The knowing of empty stillness] The knowing of empty stillness is a knowing without knowing; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is also called “numinous knowing.” The Surangama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing establish a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvana, pure and free of outflows.”
Master Hanshan’s Record of the Contemplation of the Lankavatara says:
“The mind being still and yet knowing, both true and false are left behind; this is named the self-awakened noble wisdom.”
For details see
the article “Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“The self-nature can contain all dharmas, and is named the storehouse consciousness. If thinking arises, that is the turning consciousness; it produces the six consciousnesses, goes out through the six gates, and sees the six sense objects; thus the eighteen realms all arise and function from the self-nature. If the self-nature is deviant, eighteen deviant functions arise; if the self-nature is upright, eighteen upright functions arise. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if the function is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.”

Translation: The self-nature can contain all dharmas, and so it is named the storehouse consciousness (the original nature). If the self-nature gives rise to thinking, that is the turning consciousness (the nature of consciousness), which produces the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out through the six gates (that is, the six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and see the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects). Thus the eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, six faculties, and six sense objects) are all the self-nature at work. If the self-nature is deviant, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen deviant functions; if the self-nature is upright, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen upright functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if it is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.

A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

Therefore the self-nature has its deviant (deluded) and upright (awakened) aspects, and the thinker has evil and upright functions. Cultivation is precisely to turn the self-nature from delusion to awakening, until the great enlightenment. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
When Shakyamuni Buddha, beneath the bodhi tree, saw the morning star at dawn and awakened to the Way, he said:
“How wondrous! How wondrous! All sentient beings are complete with the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks, but because of deluded thinking and clinging they cannot realize them.”

The purpose of Chan inquiry—clarifying the mind and seeing the nature—is to remove the defilements of one’s own mind and truly see the original face of the self-nature. The defilements are deluded thinking and clinging; the original face of the self-nature is the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks. If one is free of deluded thinking and clinging, one realizes one’s own Tathagata wisdom and virtue marks, and is a Buddha; otherwise one is a sentient being. Turning back to look at your own original face is simply not being hijacked by the deluded mind (the shadowy traces of the six sense objects), and thereby resting deluded thinking and clinging; and that resting is bodhi. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, the work must be carried on without interruption, until the faculties and objects fall away and one thoroughly sees the original nature.
